slides.0.title: Gin, vodka and liqueurs
slides.0.subtitle: Neutral spirit is the canvas: botanicals, fruit and sugar decide the final style
slides.1.title: Gin and vodka
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Gin
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Neutral spirit of agricultural origin flavoured with botanicals, with juniper as the predominant flavour; the EU requires at least 37.5% at bottling
slides.1.highlights.1.title: London Dry Gin
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Not a place name but a method: flavoured only by redistillation with natural botanicals, with no flavourings or colour added afterwards and minimal sugar (no more than 0.1 g per litre)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Vodka
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Highly purified neutral spirit from agricultural raw materials, often filtered through activated charcoal; the base (grain, potato, grape, etc.) affects texture and subtle flavour; the EU minimum is 37.5%
slides.1.content: “London Dry” tells you how it is made, not where.
slides.2.title: Liqueurs
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Definition
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Spirit with added sugar and flavour (fruit, herbs, spice, nuts, coffee and so on); the EU generally requires at least 100 g/L sugar and 15% alcohol, at least 250 g/L for “crème de” liqueurs and 400 g/L for crème de cassis
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Flavouring methods
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Maceration, percolation or redistillation with botanicals; herbal liqueurs (such as monastic recipes) often combine several methods
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Role on the list
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Liqueurs are often served after dinner and in cocktails; a sommelier should be able to name the base spirit, main flavour and sweetness and suggest serving neat, on ice or mixed
slides.2.content: Three points to describe any liqueur: base spirit, flavour, sweetness.
